Greedily coveting wealth and deceiving one's superiors.

Using short measures and narrow capacities, light scales and small measures.
Mixing the false with the true.
Gaining profit through craft and deceit.
Oppressing the good and making them lowly.
Brazenly deceiving the foolish.
Being greedy and never satisfied.
Cursing and swearing to seek vindication.
Given to wine and rebellious disorder.
Quarreling bitterly with one's own flesh and blood.
A man who is neither loyal nor good.
A woman who is neither gentle nor obedient.
Not living in harmony with one's spouse.
Not respecting one's husband.
Always fond of self-praise.
Given to jealousy and envy.
Lacking proper conduct toward wife and children.
Failing in propriety toward one's parents-in-law.
Treating the spirits of the ancestors with contempt.
Disobeying the commands of superiors.
Doing what is of no benefit.

Cursing themselves and cursing others.
Showing partiality, hating some and loving others.
Stepping over wells and stoves.
Jumping over food and over people.
Harming children and inducing abortion.
Acting much in secret and dark ways.
Singing and dancing on the dark days of month-end and the La festival.
Wailing and raging at the new moon daybreak.
Spitting and urinating toward the north.
Chanting and weeping toward the stove.
Also burning incense with a stove fire.
Cooking food with dirty firewood.
Rising in the night while naked.
Carrying out executions on the eight festival days.
Spitting at shooting stars, pointing at rainbows, pointing at the three luminaries, and staring long at the sun and moon.
Hunting with fire in the spring months.
Cursing viciously toward the north.
Killing turtles and striking snakes without cause.

For such offenses, the Director of Destinies, according to their gravity, takes away his years and allotted span; when the span is exhausted, he dies, and if there remain unexpiated worth, the calamity extends even to his descendants.

Moreover, those who unjustly seize the wealth of others are made to pay for it through their wives, children, and household, until death and bereavement come upon them; and if they do not suffer death and bereavement, then there befall them fire, water, and robbers...
Moreover, those who wrongfully kill others are but exchanging the sword for mutual slaughter.

Those who take wealth that is not rightfully theirs are like one who eats tainted dried meat to still his hunger, or drinks poisoned wine to quench his thirst; it is not that it does not satisfy for a moment, but death comes with it too.

When the mind gives rise to goodness, even though the good is not yet done, the auspicious spirit already follows; or when the mind gives rise to evil, even though the evil is not yet done, the inauspicious spirit already follows.

As for those who have formerly done evil and afterward repent and reform, doing no evil and practicing all good, in time they will surely obtain good fortune; this is what is meant by turning calamity into blessing.

Therefore the auspicious man speaks good, looks on good, and acts good; doing three good things a day, in three years heaven will surely send down blessing upon him. The inauspicious man speaks evil, looks on evil, and acts evil...

The Tract of the Most High on Response: Annotated, Explained, and Compiled with Case Corroboration; Vernacular Abridged Edition, Volume Four
Explanation:
Obtaining goods by coercion, or demanding that others supply them; or being fond of encroaching on others' property, or being fond of seizing it by force.
Analysis:

Whatever goods are not rightfully mine by lot, yet which I insist upon obtaining, is called 'seizing by force.' To have others supply goods for my use is called 'extorting.' To obtain the goods of others by secret craft is called 'encroaching.' To take them openly by force is called 'plundering.' Goods gained by such means are naturally hard for one to enjoy; moreover, in the future they will surely cause one to lose even the goods that rightfully belonged to one's own lot in life!

Zheng Xuan said: 'From what I have observed, this thing called money is something everyone delights in; it is something men inevitably contend for. Among flesh and blood it stirs up disputes; among the well-known it ruins their good name; merchants lose their lives for it, and the common crowd beat and kill one another for it. Yet wealth comes suddenly and vanishes suddenly; rank rises swiftly and sinks swiftly to poverty. In sum, in governing the world money brings people but little blessing and much calamity. I have examined it closely: the shape of the word for money is a 'gold' beside two 'spears'; money is truly a thing that kills men, yet most are unable to awaken to it. Ah, money! Money! In my poverty I beg you to keep me alive but cannot obtain it; I am helpless against you and can do nothing about you. In my poverty you may wish to kill me, but that too you cannot do; you are helpless against me and likewise can do nothing to me.'
Story One:

There was a man of Zhao named Wei Gongxiong. In his youth he was extremely poor and could no longer support his mother in food and clothing; husband and wife wept together over it. The next day, while sweeping the ground, he found a silver ingot weighing twenty-five taels, and so his livelihood became somewhat better. Later Wei Gongxiong became a minister, with a salary of one hundred ingots of silver. When he received his salary, he found that one twenty-five-tael ingot was missing and was about to question the official in charge of funds the next day. That night he dreamed that a spirit told him: 'On such-and-such a day, month, and year, you had already borrowed one ingot!'
Further Analysis:

One must know that even if one's lot contains wealth, if the time and fortune have not yet come, one still cannot obtain it by human effort; how much less when one's lot has no wealth at all, yet one takes money by coercion?
Story Two:

In Kunshan there was an old man surnamed Yang. One day, sitting before his own gate, he saw a woman passing by who dropped a silver hairpin onto the stone-paved street; and when the hairpin fell to the ground it rang out with a clatter! Old Yang hurried forward to look, but to his surprise there was no hairpin; instead he saw an earthworm. Old Yang stood puzzled in place, pacing back and forth a long while without leaving. Suddenly a man came by and picked up the silver hairpin from the ground. Old Yang called out loudly, 'That is my hairpin that fell!' The gentleman knew old Yang was lying and, taking no notice of him, went on his way. Old Yang pursued him closely from behind, so the gentleman could only take out two fen of silver, telling old Yang to use half to buy fish and half to buy wine, and saying to him, 'Old sir, do not keep pestering me; use this silver to buy wine and cook fish and pass a merry night.' When old Yang returned home he told his daughter-in-law to cook the fish; as he was warming the wine, the neighbor's cat suddenly dashed in and carried off the fish, and the daughter-in-law struck the cat with a staff, thereby knocking over the wine; she also broke the dish that held the fish!

One should realize that when the silver hairpin turned into an earthworm, old Yang ought to have awakened. But old Yang was far too greedy and still persisted in demanding it by force; so he had not the good fortune to enjoy either the wine or the fish; how could he manage to eat them? Alas, old Yang truly was a man of thin fortune! A single small matter came to such a pass; as for other greater matters, one need not ask to know how it would go!
Story Three:

In Yin County, Zhejiang, there was a man surnamed Lu who was very wealthy but crafty and deceitful in nature. His neighbor, a Mr. Zheng, had some family property, and Lu secretly contrived to seize it; he tore down Zheng's house and made of it his own mansion and garden, leaving only one fine tree that Zheng's family had planted. Later Lu had a son who, at the age of five, still could not speak. Suddenly one day the son pointed at that tree and said, 'Tree! Tree! You are still here today!' The family was greatly startled, and after the child finished speaking he became mute once more. Lu exhausted every remedy to heal his son, but the son could never utter a single word. When the son grew up he was wild and lustful, giving himself to drink and pleasure, and spent all of Lu's fortune before he died. Everyone said, 'This child is the reappearance of Zheng, born into the world to demand repayment of the debt from Lu!'
Using violent force to plunder the goods of others so as to grow rich.

Officials who exploit the people and secretly plunder public funds, or rich tyrants and evil gentry who lend money at heavy interest; these are all acts of plunder and seizure. Wealth gained by such means is the karmic evil that breaks up families and scatters people, making wives weep and children cry. How can one enjoy such wealth with peace of mind? Has one not heard the principle of the piggy bank? In the Book of Han the piggy bank is called 'hou', which is what is now called a 'dumb gourd.' It is made of pottery with a single opening on top through which coins can be put in; once the coins go in, they cannot be taken out. People use it to save money, and when the money has filled it, they break the bank open to take the coins out, and so it is called a 'piggy bank.' While it is gathering money it only fears it is not full; when it is full, it must be broken before stopping. At that point the bank is broken and the money gone, and both become nothing. So the more one hoards, the more one loses; it is no different from the piggy bank!

In the Song dynasty, when Wen Yanbo, Duke of Lu, was serving as chief judge of Chang'an, he came one day to Benniu Yan, where there was an ox that suddenly spoke in human speech: 'I served in court alongside Wen Yanbo for twenty years; today how do I have the face to see him again!' The soldier in charge of Benniu Yan reported the matter to Wen Yanbo, who ordered the soldier to bring the ox; the ox lay prostrate on the ground with its head bowed, its tears flowing like rain. Wen Yanbo sighed deeply and said, 'My colleague, in life because he secretly plundered public funds, today has met this retribution!' Thereupon he ordered the household accountant to bring out twenty strings of cash to add fodder for the ox.

One must know that the money of the government is the tax paid by the people, and that Wen Yanbo's colleague, turning into an ox to build the dike, was repaying the debt he owed to the people. Seeing this case, one should reflect upon it carefully!

In Suzhou there was an oil seller who, one day while selling oil, passed a wealthy household and saw a five-year-old child wearing a red cap with a golden lock at the chest; he thereupon conceived an evil thought. He carried the child off to a secluded place and killed him, then took the gold ornaments, and suddenly became rich. Later he had a son whose appearance closely resembled the child he had killed, and he came to detest the child. When the child reached the age of five, it was the height of summer and very hot; the oil seller happened to doze off, and the child pulled out the silver hairpin stuck in his topknot and used it to stab playfully at the oil seller's chest. The oil seller thought it was a fly stinging him, raised his hand and slapped; and the silver hairpin pierced right through his chest, killing him on the spot.

Seeing this case, parents who delight in adorning their sons and daughters with gold ornaments and jewels should truly reform this habit; even if one is wealthy, one should not be ostentatious, lest one draw covetous eyes and invite the calamity of losing one's life!
Using crafty and deceitful means to procure one's own promotion.

A superior man, once he enters officialdom, should take loyalty, uprightness, fairness, and incorruptibility as his own proper duty. If, in order to seek promotion, he uses crafty and deceitful means, such a heart and mind is truly improper! Such a man in the court will surely not be loyal; as an official he will not be fair; and if he is sent out as a local official managing the affairs of the people, how can he remain incorrupt and self-possessed? Therefore the Most High here issues special warning. Moreover, a person's achievements, fame, rank, and emolument in a single lifetime are fixed by heaven at birth; even if he labors all his life to seek them, he cannot add the slightest bit. He will only make himself a laughingstock for the wise and be rebuked by ghosts and spirits!

In the time of Emperor Xiaowu of Liu-Song, the three men Dai Faxing, Dai Mingbao, and Chao Shangzhi held such power in the court that they could call the wind and summon the rain; none of those whom they recommended and brought in was ever rejected. People thought that through the recommendation of these three, one's official career would surely be smooth. Only Gu Kaizhi disagreed. He said, 'A person's official emolument is arranged by heaven long before; it is not something that stratagem and craft can transfer or change. One can only be respectful and cautious and strictly keep to one's lot; if one hopes for luck, one merely loses the lot one ought to keep; it has nothing at all to do with the gaining or losing of office.'

Someone, seeing this case, asked me, 'But nowadays it often happens that people who use strategy obtain office; what is the principle of this?' I replied, 'That too is his fate! If it were not that office and emolument lie in his lot, whatever means he used would be futile. Although one may capture birds and beasts by craft and deceit, a superior man would never do such a thing!'
Words of Praise:

Qian Bangqi of Dantu in the Qing dynasty once said, 'Even if a person has the ability to reach heaven, he cannot contend with the ordained fate. Yet only the practice of hidden virtue can surely turn back the ordained fate; and what is done yesterday has its effect today; what is done in the morning answers in the evening. The retribution in the unseen realm is swiftest, and the scrutiny of the spirits is most clear. This truly is the swiftest shortcut; anyone with a willing mind need only try and he will know!'
If reward and punishment are too light or too heavy, that is being unjust.

If, in rewarding the meritorious or punishing the guilty, one errs in the slightest, that is being unfair; and since public justice no longer exists, the people's hearts will not submit. Not only does this fail to reward merit and punish guilt, but it instead accumulates resentment and invites calamity!
Story:

Zhuge Kongming of Shu Han said, 'My heart is like a balance; I cannot lighten it for anyone or weight it against anyone.' Chen Shou praised him, saying, 'Kongming may be called a model of utmost loyalty and service to the age! Though a man were his enemy, if he had merit he was sure to be rewarded; and one who broke the law and was negligent in performing his duties, though a relative, was sure to be punished. One who confessed his guilt was worthy of forgiveness, and though his offense were grave, he was sure to be released; but one who with crafty words excused his offense, though his crime were light, was surely put to death without mercy. Hence all the generals of Shu at the time were able to lay down their lives for the state; even Wei Yan, that traitor to the state, had no complaint under Kongming's leadership; and the two generals Li Ping and Liao Li, though stripped of office by Kongming and sentenced to lifelong exile on the frontier, had not a word of resentment. Therefore those who hold the power of reward and punishment should take Kongming as their model!'
In ease and pleasure one should be moderate and not go to excess.

Ease and pleasure are what everyone delights in! The Book of Rites says, 'Pleasure must not be excessive, and desires must not be indulged.' The Discourses of the States says, 'When the people are toilsome they think of goodness; when they are at ease they think of indulgence.' The intent is simply to keep the people from wallowing in ease. Mencius also says, 'One thrives in anxiety and hardship, and perishes in ease and pleasure.' This too is to keep people from wallowing in ease and pleasure; how much more when ease and pleasure are excessive and utterly without restraint! But what the world calls ease and pleasure, the greatest of it is no more than wine, lust, wealth, and anger. People today who are addicted to wine disregard their bodies; lustful of beauty they disregard their illness; greedy for wealth they disregard their kin; and in quarrels they disregard their very lives. Before encountering these situations, they are able to understand such principles and to dissuade others; but when they encounter these realms themselves, they commit them in confusion. This is what is meant by being able to see through it but not able to endure it. If one can embody the four words 'ease and pleasure beyond measure,' then one's habits and nature will be changed, and these familiar realms of wine, lust, wealth, and anger will be forgotten; having cultivated to the point where desires are few and the mind pure, one can stand peerless between heaven and earth!

Once, when the monk Master Zhi Gong was conversing with Emperor Wu of Liang about music, Master Zhi Gong asked the emperor to have some prisoners brought out from the jail for a test. He ordered each prisoner to hold a cup filled with water and pace back and forth beneath the hall, warning them, 'If the water in your cup does not spill, I will commute your death sentence.' Then he had music played to divert the prisoners' attention and see whether they would be distracted. After a long while, not a drop of water had spilled from the prisoners' cups. Emperor Wu sighed and said, 'Did you not hear the music?' The prisoners all said, 'No.' National Master Zhi Gong said, 'They were afraid of being beheaded and fearful lest the water in their cups spill; how could they hear the music?'
If a person can, like those prisoners, constantly hold a heart of fear, then the mind of ease and pleasure will naturally not arise!

Mr. Yu Tieqiao said, 'Diligent like one carrying bricks and tiles, cautious like one facing the deep abyss and treading on thin ice; the sages and heroes of old have all been thus diligent. Who am I, that I should dare to be so carefree and lead so idle and luxurious a life!' The Book of Changes says, 'The movement of heaven is vigorous; the superior man thereby strengthens himself without ceasing.' If a person is unwilling to strengthen himself, then before an urgent or personally vital matter arises he will want to pass his days in ease and wandering. But one who is determined to strengthen himself will find that the tasks he ought to do are endless. Only when one feels there are not enough hours in the day is there any spare time for amusement; thus naturally one does not dare to let go into indolence!

Fan Wenzheng of the Song dynasty said, 'Every night when I go to bed, I am certain to consider whether the salary the state gives me today is proportionate to what I did in the daytime. If they are proportionate, then I can sleep soundly in peace without shame or disgrace; if they are not, then I cannot sleep all night.'

In the Yuan dynasty there were two students of the Imperial College, born in the same year, month, day, and hour, who also passed the provincial examination at the same time and were appointed to office on the same day. One was given the post of professor of Ezhou, the other the post of professor of Huangzhou. Before long the professor of Huangzhou died. The professor of Ezhou was greatly frightened and made ready all his funeral affairs; but after several days he still did not die. So he prepared gifts and went to offer condolences to the professor of Huangzhou, weeping before the coffin, 'You and I were born in the same year, month, day, and hour, and our careers and positions have been the same; today you have gone before me. Even if I were to die now, I would be seven days later than you. If you have a spirit, you should appear to me in a dream and tell me!' That night he dreamed that the professor of Huangzhou told him, 'You, because you are frugal and thrifty in everything, will live long; whereas I, because I consumed to excess without restraint, died young!'

In the Liang dynasty there was a wealthy man surnamed Yu who built a high tower facing the main thoroughfare. From morning to night he and beautiful women sang, feasted, gambled, and played chess in the tower; the winners covered their mouths and laughed. It happened that three passersby were walking beneath the Yu's tower when a rotting rat fell from the beak of a hawk and landed right on their heads. The three passersby looked up and saw the people above covering their mouths and laughing. They were furious and said, 'The Yu family is wealthy and has enjoyed itself too long; we did not offend him, yet he has insulted us!' Thereupon they gathered a crowd and killed the entire Yu household.

Mr. Gu Xichou said, 'Even if the Yu's tower had not faced the thoroughfare, some strange calamity would still have befallen them. The proverb says that pride and excess bring many disasters, and the causes of disaster are not all the same; yet among the disasters of pride and excess, the disaster of lusting after women is the most severe and the swiftest. Hence guarding against lust for women is most important!' Wu Shi, the man of practical affairs, also said, 'Skin wrapping bone and flesh, all foulness, / Yet each strains to be alluring and deceives; / Heroes of a thousand ages meet their fall through this, / In a hundred years all share one grave of dust.' If a person can understand this principle and, together with the annotations in this book on 'Seeing a beauty and privately coveting her' and 'Lust to excess,' thoroughly understand them, and with reverence keep the teachings and prohibitions, maintaining the contemplation of emptiness, he will not sink into the enjoyment of ease and invite disaster.
Being harsh and cruel to one's subordinates or servants.

Officials who cruelly abuse their subordinates and the people, or masters who excessively punish and flog the household servants; these are acts of harsh cruelty. The matter of officials in high position abusing their subordinates and the common people has already been explained in detail earlier in this book; so now we will only explain the part about the master of a household treating his servants.

The Buddha told Sigala: 'In treating their servants, all people in the world should understand five things. First, they should first know their cold, heat, hunger, and thirst, and then have them work. Second, if they are ill, one should treat them. Third, if they commit offenses, one may not flog or punish them at will; one should first ask the reason and then administer discipline. Whom one can forgive, forgive; whom one cannot forgive, instruct and punish. Fourth, if they have a little personal wealth of their own, one may not seize it for oneself. Fifth, in distributing things to servants, one should be fair and not partial.'

Master Yuan's Model for the World says, 'The natural endowments of servants are mostly somewhat inferior to those of ordinary people, so they often make mistakes, and moreover are forgetful; sometimes they forget entirely what they were told. Most are also stubborn and often think themselves right. Some servants are also hot-tempered, speaking without regard for rank, not understanding the principle of superiority and inferiority. Therefore, when the head of a household sets them to work, he should treat them with a generous heart; use much instruction and do not be angry, so that the master's own heart may also be at ease. Even when servants commit offenses and should be punished and reproved, one should question them calmly and with equanimity; once they have been reproved, in employing them afterward one should keep a normal tone and expression, so that no other trouble arises. As for women, whose dispositions are narrow, stubborn, and willful, the head of the household should frequently instruct and teach them. The young people of the family also may not beat servants at will; if a matter arises, they should report it to the head of the household. If a servant is truly a vicious, coarse, and evil person, one should also send him away by a proper means, and not treat him with stern severity, lest such a person later bear a grudge and take revenge!'

Mr. Yu Tieqiao said, 'In treating inferiors, harsh cruelty is indeed improper; but to indulge them and let them act without restraint is even more improper! One often sees the servants of noble and high officials arrogant and unreasonable, and even exalted to the skies; when they go out they ride swift horses and wear bright clothing, and when they return home they gamble and drink; or when a guest comes to call they sit there without rising to receive him; or when a relative comes to visit they refuse and will not announce it. Thus distinguished guests and relatives leave in anger, while those of lower station or connection leave bitter and grieved; or even these fierce servants invent pretexts for trouble, rely on their master's power, and defraud others of money abroad, while the master turns a deaf ear. In the end it comes to all turning away and all kindred estranged, offending so many friends and drawing so much resentment! Therefore one must be extremely cautious!'

Tao Yuanming, the great poet of the Jin dynasty, admonished his son, 'Your daily work keeps you too busy to have spare time to look after yourself; now I am sending a servant to help you in gathering firewood and carrying water, to lighten your burden. But the servant is also another person's child, and you should treat him well!'
